title: GPU Egress Sidecar and Proxy Mitigations for Multi-Account Burst
author: Priya Menon
content:
Summary:
This document defines the GPU egress sidecar + proxy pattern we use to protect tenant egress, provide accurate per-tenant accounting, and mitigate sudden burst traffic across cloud accounts. It includes design rationale, Terraform module interface, CI/CD image requirements, runtime configuration, SLOs and throttling rules, and an operational runbook for incidents and testing.

Context and motivation:
- Problem: GPU-backed inference pools occasionally generate large egress spikes (model downloads, large embedding uploads, telemetry, or customers issuing batch jobs). When pools are shared across multiple cloud accounts or projects, these spikes can saturate NAT gateways, exhaust egress quotas, or cause noisy-neighbor billing and throttling.
- Goals: provide predictable egress behavior, fine-grained per-tenant accounting, quick mitigation for bursts, and a secure, auditable proxy path that integrates with our IaC and CI/CD workflows.

Scope and non-goals:
- Scope: multi-account GPU pools, tenant-facing inference services, dedicated NAT/egress accounting, Terraform modules for sidecar deployment, CI pipelines for sidecar image promotion, and runbooks for surge events.
- Non-goals: egress encryption (handled by TLS end-to-end at application layer) and upstream provider-level quotas on partner clouds (we surface them but do not control provider limits).

Architecture overview:
1) Sidecar proxy (per-pod or per-vm lightweight process)
   - Runs alongside inference runtime container as an iptables redirector or transparent HTTP/HTTPS forward proxy.
   - Responsibilities: enforce per-tenant egress token, annotate flows for billing, perform simple rate limiting, short-circuit cache for common model artifacts, and emit metrics to our telemetry pipeline.
2) Account-level aggregator
   - A small fleet of regional egress-aggregator instances (managed by auto-scaling groups) that accept proxied traffic from sidecars and forward to internet with centralized NAT. Implements more advanced buffering, bucket-based throttling, and cross-account fair-share decisions.
3) NAT / Egress Gateway cluster
   - Manages cloud NATs (NAT Gateway / Cloud NAT) and handles failover across subnetworks. Exports per-ENI/elastic-IP usage to billing pipeline.
4) Control plane connectors
   - IAM service account rotation for sidecars, config distribution via SSM/Secrets Manager, and Terraform modules to declare account bindings and routing.

Key design decisions:
- Transparent redirect vs explicit proxy: we prefer explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxy for TLS termination avoidance and simpler multi-protocol handling (TCP/UDP too). Transparent redirect is supported as fallback for legacy workloads.
- Per-tenant token in egress header: sidecar injects X-Redwood-Tenant and signed egress-token so downstream aggregators can attribute bytes reliably.
- Two-tier throttling: lightweight local token-bucket at sidecar (<100ms enforcement) plus global account buckets in aggregator for fairness across instances.
- Cache model artifacts close to runtime: sidecar local disk cache + regionally shared object cache to avoid repeated downloads to internet.

Terraform module: redwood/gpu-egress-sidecar (inputs/outputs)
- Module purpose: deploy sidecar DaemonSet or VM-agent with associated IAM roles, security groups, and routing rules.
- Inputs (table):
  name: module name identifier as string
  deployment_mode: [daemonset | vm-agent]
  sidecar_image: container image URI to use
  cache_size_gb: numeric (string) - disk cache size per node
  local_rate_limit_mbps: per-instance default rate limit (string, Mbps)
  aggregator_endpoint: URL for regional aggregator
  iam_role_arn: role used by sidecar for config fetch and token signing
  allowed_outbound_ports: CSV of ports
  nat_public_ip_pool: list of allowed elastic IPs for egress (stringified list)
- Outputs (table):
  sidecar_daemonset_name: name
  iam_role_binding: arn
  vpc_route_patch_id: id
  aggregator_security_group: id
- Example usage snippet (YAML-ish):
  module "gpu_egress_sidecar" {
    source = "git::ssh://git.redwood.com/infra-modules//gpu-egress-sidecar?ref=v1.2.0"
    name = "inference-egress-a"
    deployment_mode = "daemonset"
    sidecar_image = "ghcr.io/redwood/egress-sidecar:2025-02-08"
    cache_size_gb = "12"
    local_rate_limit_mbps = "400"
    aggregator_endpoint = "https://egress-agg.us-east-1.redwood.internal"
    iam_role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/egress-sidecar-role"
    allowed_outbound_ports = "80,443,853"
    nat_public_ip_pool = "[\"34.12.34.10\", \"34.12.34.11\"]"
  }

Sidecar runtime config (defaults)
- config file path: /etc/redwood/egress-sidecar/config.yaml
- default settings (key: value list):
  - local_token_bucket_capacity: "1000000"  # bytes
  - local_refill_rate_bps: "50000000"       # bytes/sec ~50Mbps
  - header_injection: "X-Redwood-Tenant"
  - cache_eviction_policy: "lru"
  - health_check_path: "/healthz"
  - telemetry_flush_interval_seconds: "10"

CI/CD and image promotion rules
1) Image build pipeline (Buildkite):
   - Trigger: changes to infra/egress-sidecar repository or security patches to base image.
   - Steps: unit tests -> static analysis (C/C++/Go or Python lint) -> container image build -> SBOM generation -> vulnerable dependency scan -> canary image push to ephemeral registry -> integration tests in ephemeral GPU sandbox -> promote to staging registry.
2) Promotion gating:
   - Staging -> production promotion requires: passing integration tests, review from networking owner, and signing by SREs.
   - Image tag pattern: yyyy-mm-dd-commitsha (promoted tags for production use "prod-YYYYMMDD-vN").
3) Terraform module release:
   - Module releases are semver. Any change affecting IAM, routing, or NAT must have a cross-team review and an ADR link in the module CHANGELOG.

Operational SLOs and metrics to monitor
- Availability: sidecar DaemonSet rollout success >= 99.9% per region per week.
- Latency: proxy-handshake added latency < 5ms p50 and < 20ms p99 under normal load.
- Egress accounting accuracy: attribution mismatch < 0.1% over 24h window.
- Throttling effectiveness: during simulated bursts, account-level drop rate <= 2% while maintaining aggregate fairness.
- Key metrics: sidecar.health, sidecar.cache_hit_ratio, sidecar.local_throttle_count, aggregator.bucket_balance, nat.ip_utilization, egress.bytes_by_tenant, egress.errors_5xx.

Runbook: Egress surge (priority P1)
1) Detection triggers:
   - NAT public IP 90% utilization sustained for 5m OR
   - sudden rise in egress.bytes_by_tenant > 3x baseline for > 2m OR
   - aggregate 5xx egress errors across aggregator > 1% for 5m.
2) Initial mitigation (0-5m):
   - Page oncall (eng-infra).
   - Enable soft-throttle mode via control plane (set aggregator_global_limit = 80% of baseline) to reduce outgoing rate.
   - Identify top-10 tenant contributors from egress.bytes_by_tenant.
3) Triage (5-15m):
   - For each top tenant, check recent config: job runs, model downloads, scheduled batch windows.
   - If a tenant has runaway traffic, apply tenant-specific token-bucket reduction in aggregator (example command):
     curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $CTRL_API' -d '{"tenant":"t-123","limit_mbps":50}' https://egress-agg.us-east-1.redwood.internal/api/token-buckets
   - If traffic is due to model downloads, enable cache prewarming for that model in the aggregator to reduce outbound bytes.
4) Recovery (15m-1h):
   - Gradually raise global limit while validating nat.ip_utilization and 5xx rates.
   - If NAT IP pool exhausted, coordinate with cloud-ops to allocate extra elastic IPs or failover to secondary region.
5) Post-incident (1h+):
   - Run automated attribution audit (compare egress.bytes_by_tenant to sidecar emitted events) and store report.
   - Create incident summary and attach to postmortem board.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-deploy)
- Unit and integration tests for sidecar (mock aggregator, simulate partial packet loss).
- Load test: 1.5x baseline sustained for 30 minutes with synthetic tenant distribution to validate throttling.
- Failure injection: simulate aggregator restart and ensure sidecars buffer or fallback to direct egress with alert.
- IaC static checks: terraform fmt, validate, and a policy-as-code scan (OPA) for IAM scope.
- Security review: SBOM inspection and image CVE threshold (no critical CVEs).

Security and compliance considerations
- Sidecars authenticate to aggregator using short-lived mTLS certificates provisioned via our internal PKI.
- Egress headers are signed; sensitive tenant identifiers are hashed in logs.
- Audit logs for token issuance and aggregator decisions retained for 90 days by default (configurable per-customer for Dedicated/Private).

Operational ownership and run cadence
- Service owner: eng-infra networking subteam (primary oncall rotation).
- Tier-2 support: infra SREs for escalation.
- Weekly reports: egress utilization digest every Monday to capacity-planning channel.

Appendix: related knobs and quick reference
- Quick CLI snippets:
  - Check aggregator bucket status: curl -s https://egress-agg.us-east-1.redwood.internal/api/buckets | jq
  - Reduce tenant limit: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"tenant":"t-456","limit_mbps":20}' $AGG_API/tokens
- Default cache paths: /var/lib/redwood/egress-cache, cache size per node defined in module param cache_size_gb.
- Ownership matrix:
  - sidecar code and CI: eng-developer-experience (codeowner: @lina-zhang)
  - aggregator ops and autoscaling: eng-sre (codeowner: @ethan-rivera)
  - IAM & accounts: eng-infra cloud-accounts team (owner: @marco-alvarez)

End of document.
